activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Arlo looked out the window. The grass was gone. White snow was everywhere. "No school today," said Mama. "It is a snow day." Arlo clapped his hands. He wanted to play in the backyard.

He ran outside in his slippers. His toes felt cold right away. "Ow," said Arlo. He ran back in. "My feet are cold because I have no boots," he said. Mama smiled. "Yes. Snow is very cold. Boots keep you warm."

Mama helped him put on his boots. She helped him tie the laces. She pulled each tie tight. "Now my feet are warm," said Arlo. He stomped in the snow. Crunch, crunch, crunch.

Then Arlo saw his pet dog, Bingo. Bingo was shivering. "Why is Bingo cold?" Arlo asked. "Because dogs get cold too," said Mama. She put a little coat on Bingo. Bingo wagged his tail. Arlo patted his soft ears. Together they made a big snowball. It grew and grew. "Best snow day ever," said Arlo, and he threw his mittens up in the air.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Leon sat in a big chair. It was his first haircut at the salon. His mom stood right next to him and held his hand.

The hairdresser, Miss Jo, put a cape on Leon. The cape had rainbows on it. "Snip, snip," went the scissors. A little piece of hair fell down. It landed on the cape. "Look, Mom," said Leon. "The snip makes my hair fall!" Mom smiled and said, "Yes, one snip, one little piece."

Miss Jo kept going. One snip, one piece. Two snips, two pieces. Three snips, three pieces. The hair fell down like soft rain. Leon watched every piece. His head felt lighter and lighter. Soon he got tired of sitting so still, so Miss Jo gave him a squeeze toy to hold.

At last the haircut was done. Miss Jo brushed off the cape. Leon looked in the mirror. His hair was short and neat. "New hair!" he said. Then Mom picked him up for a big hug. At home, Dad was going to cook pasta for dinner. Leon sat in his small chair, still in his socks, and told Dad all about it. "One snip, one piece," he said. "And now I have new hair!"

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Owen was grumpy. He did not want to see Doctor Paz today. His tummy felt funny and the office smelled like soap.

First, Doctor Paz held up a picture. "Cover one eye," she said. Owen covered his eye with his hand. Now he could not see the duck with that eye. He took his hand away. The duck came back! "My eyes see it," Owen said. "My hand was in the way."

Then she looked in his ears. "Say aah," she said. Owen said, "Aah." Doctor Paz rang a little bell. Ding! Owen's ears heard it. Then she put a cotton ball over the bell. Now it was quiet. "The cotton stops the sound," said Owen. Doctor Paz laughed. "You are a smart patient."

Next came a taste test. Doctor Paz gave Owen a tiny cup. "Taste this." Owen tasted it. "Yuck! It is bitter!" Then he pinched his nose and tasted again. Now he could not taste it at all. He let go of his nose. Yuck came back! "My nose helps my tongue," Owen said. "That is silly!" Doctor Paz smiled. "Your nose and tongue are a team."

At the end, she gave him a warm sticker of a truck. Owen touched it with his fingers. It felt bumpy. He sniffed his bread snack in his bag. It smelled good. On the way home he said, "Dad, can we build a doctor office at home?" Dad said, "Yes. But I get the bell." Ding!

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Anna sat at the big table. The soup was hot. Mama said, "Hold hands first." Anna held Papa's hand. She held Grandma's hand too.

Anna wanted to say the blessing. She was too young to know all the words. Her mouth opened. Nothing came out. Grandma smiled and pointed at the cow bowl. "Count with me," Grandma said. "One, thank you for the cow. Two, thank you for the corn. Three, thank you for us."

Anna counted with Grandma. "One. Two. Three." She did not need big words. She only needed to count good things.

The next night, Anna held hands first. She pointed at the bread. "One, thank you for the bread," she said. "Two, thank you for the soup." Then she stopped. She looked at Baby Ben. He was too small to eat soup.

"Three, thank you for Ben," Anna said. Ben banged his spoon. Everyone laughed. Papa gave Anna the first piece of bread. "You said it all by yourself," he said. Anna took a big, warm bite.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Edouard found a red book at school. On the cover he saw little black marks. "What are those?" he asked. His friend Mia said, "They are words. Words tell you things." Edouard opened the book. He held it tight. Page one, page two, page three. He turned the pages from front to back. On page three was a soft white rabbit. "A pet," said Edouard. "I want this book forever."

He asked his teacher, "Can I keep it?" She said, "No, Edouard. This book is from the library. You can take it home. Then you bring it back so other kids can read it too." Edouard felt sad. But he took the book home. He smelled the pages. They smelled like paper and sun. He read the rabbit book every night.

On Friday, his mom said, "Time to take the book back." Edouard held it tight one more time. Then he put it in his bag. At school, he gave it back. "Why do I give it back?" he asked. "So Sam can read it next." At circle time, Sam held the red book. He opened it to the rabbit. Edouard smiled and said, "Page one, page two, page three."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Claire ran to the toy shelf at daycare. The red truck was not there.

"Where is the red truck?" she asked.

Teacher Sam pointed. "Ben has it now. You can have it later, after snack time."

Claire looked out the window. The sky was cloudy. "Later is a long time," she said.

"Not too long," said Teacher Sam. "We play now. We eat later. Then the truck is free."

Claire went to the blocks. She played a game with Mia. They stacked the blocks up, up, up.

"Yesterday the truck was mine," said Claire. "Today it is Ben's. Tomorrow maybe it is mine again."

"That's right," said Teacher Sam.

Snack time came. Ben put the truck on the shelf. Claire ate her crackers slowly. Then she ran to the shelf.

The red truck was there. "Later came!" said Claire. "The truck is mine now."

She pushed it across the floor. "Now, now, now!" she said.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Zoey wanted to build a fish at daycare. She found paper shapes in a box. There were circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles.

She picked a big circle for the fish body. Then she tried to make a tail with a square. The square corners stuck out. "That looks funny," said her friend Ben.

Zoey looked at the picture of a fish on the wall. The tail had pointy ends and straight sides. "A triangle has pointy ends," she thought. She pulled a triangle from the box and put it on the circle. Now the tail looked just right. "The triangle fits because the tail is pointy," she said. Then she glued two small circles on top. Would they be good eyes? Yes! The eyes were round like the circles.

Next she wanted to make fins. Which shape had two long sides? She held up a rectangle. It was long on top and long on the side too. She put one rectangle on the fish's back. It looked like a perfect little fin. She added a square at the bottom for a fin too. The square had four sides, all the same.

Ben put the fish on the wall for everyone to see. "You were so brave to try new shapes," he said. Zoey tapped the triangle tail with her finger. It felt smooth and pointy. "Look," she said. "A circle, a triangle, a rectangle, and a square. My fish has them all!"

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Elizabeth saw a big butterfly on the art table. It was blue and gold. She wanted to make one too.

She needed the glue. Ben had the glue. Elizabeth grabbed it fast. Ben's paper went crooked. It was not straight anymore. His butterfly wings fell off.

"One, two, three," said Elizabeth. She picked up the wings. She looked at Ben. "Sorry," she said.

Ben gave her the glue. "Thank you," said Elizabeth.

The glue was sticky and hard to squeeze. "Help, please," she said. Teacher Maya came and helped her hands. Squeeze, squeeze. One wing, two wings.

"Now it is straight," said Elizabeth. "Because I said sorry and please."

Ben smiled and stuck on one gold dot.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Alexander stood at the bus stop with his red coat. The bus would come soon. He wanted to zip his coat all by himself.

He pushed the zipper up. It went crooked and stopped. "Why won't it go?" he asked. He looked down. The two sides were not in the little slot together. One side was out.

He pulled the zipper all the way down. He put both sides into the slot. He heard a small click. Then he pushed the slider up, up, up. The zipper moved like a slow turtle. But it moved!

"My coat is zipped! I did it!" he said. Mama clapped. "You win, Alexander!" she said.

The bus came round the corner. Alexander was tired from trying, but he smiled. He got on the bus with his warm coat on. "I can zip it myself now," he said.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay at Olivier's house. "I will stay for one whole week," said Grandpa. Olivier wanted to know how long a week was. Was it as long as a day? Was it as long as a nap?

Olivier had an idea. He made a big paper sign. He drew seven suns on it. "Why seven suns?" asked Grandpa. "You will see," said Olivier. He hung the sign on the kitchen door.

Every morning, Grandpa would cook eggs. Then Olivier would look at the sign. One morning was gone, so he crossed out one sun. "Look, Grandpa! One sun is gone. That is one day." The next morning, he crossed out another sun. Then another, and another. The week got littler and littler.

Soon only one sun was left. Olivier felt worried. Would Grandpa leave forever? "When all the suns are gone, do you go away for always?" he asked. Grandpa smiled. "A week always ends. But a new week can start. And I can come back."

The last morning came. Grandpa cooked the eggs. Olivier crossed out the last sun. The sign had no suns at all. "The week is all done!" he said. Grandpa gave him a big hug at the park gate. Then Olivier ran home to draw seven new suns.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Eleanor ran to the park with her red ball. Then the ball rolled into the bushes. "Oh no," she said. She wanted it back.

Eleanor used her eyes to look. She saw green leaves and no ball. She used her ears to listen. She heard a small bump, bump. The ball was still rolling! Eleanor followed the sound with her ears.

A curly dog ran up too. The dog used its nose to sniff. Sniff, sniff, under the bench. The dog pushed the ball out with its nose. Eleanor reached out her hand and touched the ball. It was bumpy and warm.

"Thank you, dog," she said. She gave the dog a pat. Then she held the ball tight with both hands, so it would not roll away again.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Henri stood by a big table at the hall. Lots of people were there. Henri's grandma held his hand. "We say our blessing now," she said. Henri felt worried. He did not know the words yet.

"Watch first," said Grandma. "Then you can join in." Everyone at the table held hands. Their hands made a big ring. The ring went all around the long table, like a road over a hill.

Then everyone closed their eyes. They took a big breath. And they all said the words together. "Thank you for our food. Thank you for our friends." Their voices sounded thick and warm, like a big soft blanket.

Henri listened. The words were short. He said them in his head. Then the big breath came again. Everyone closed their eyes one more time. This time Henri said the words too. "Thank you for our food. Thank you for our friends." He said every word. Grandma squeezed his hand. Then bread came around, and Henri took a warm piece. "I said it," he told Grandma. She smiled and gave him some honey on top.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Sofia carried her towel down to the pool. The pool was right by the big beach. She could hear the waves.

"Today I will swim!" said Sofia. A boy named Sam was there too. He had a furry dog on a towel. The dog was waiting for him.

Sofia got in the water. It came up to her chin. She put her face in. The water went up her nose. It hurt! She coughed and coughed. "Why did that happen?" she asked.

Sam was blowing bubbles in the water. "Watch me," he said. He put his face in. Bubbles came out of his nose. No coughing!

So Sofia took a big breath. She put her face in the water. She blew bubbles out of her nose. The water stayed out! No coughing at all.

"Look, Dad!" she called. "My nose blows air! That keeps the water away!" She did it again. Bubbles, bubbles, bubbles. Up she came, smiling wide.

"Can we come back tomorrow?" she asked. Dad laughed. "Yes, little fish." The furry dog wagged its tail, and Sam clapped for her. Sofia splashed her feet. "Bubble time again!" she shouted, and down went her face.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Bennett stood in the pool changing room. His tummy was wet. His legs were wet too. His daddy held a big towel.

Bennett tried to put on his shirt. The shirt stuck. It would not go down. "Why will it not go on?" he asked.

Daddy patted him with the towel. The towel drank up the water. Bennett's tummy was dry now. Was that why the shirt stuck before? Bennett tried the shirt again. This time it slid right down. "Wet skin is sticky," said Bennett. "Dry skin is not sticky."

Daddy laughed and nodded. Bennett patted his own arms with the towel. He liked how soft it felt. Soon his legs were dry too. His pants went on fast, zip zip.

Bennett picked up his swim bag. He put his wet swimsuit inside. "The suit is wet because I swam in the pool," he said. He was not sad that swim time was over. Next week he would come back.

At the door, Bennett waved at the pool. "Bye bye, water," he called. "I will keep practicing my kicks."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma was coming today! Anna jumped in the kitchen. "She will stay for one, two, three, four, five, six, seven sleeps," said Mama. Anna held up seven fingers. Seven sleeps was a lot!

Anna made a chart. It had seven paper cups on it. Each cup was for one sleep. "When you rip a cup off, that sleep is done," said Anna. That night, Anna ripped one cup. Six left!

Grandma ate pancakes with Anna. Grandma made messy flour hills. Anna made messy flour hills too. They laughed and laughed. Each night, Anna ripped one more cup. Six, five, four, three, two, one.

On the last night, one cup was left. Anna ripped it off slow. "Zero cups," she said. "Zero sleeps. That means you go home today." Grandma hugged her tight. "Bring the cups when you visit me, Anna."

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Brielle woke up and looked out the window. The sun was out. "It is sunny today," she said. She put on her little yellow hat. The hat kept the sun off her nose.

Brielle wanted to play outside. She ran to the door, fast. But the sky got dark. Big drops fell. Drip, drip, drip. "Now it is rainy," said Brielle. She could not wear her sunny hat in the rain. Her hat would get all wet.

Mama gave her red rain boots and a blue raincoat. Brielle put them on. She stepped outside. The rain fell on her hood. Her feet stayed dry in the boots. The rain did not get in.

Then the wind came. It blew her hood off her head. "It is windy too," said Brielle. She held her hood with one hand. The wind could not take it now.

Later the rain turned soft and white. Snowflakes fell on her sleeve. "It is snowy," said Brielle. She met her friend Bella outside. They caught snowflakes on their mittens.

"The snow is cold," said Bella. Brielle looked at her warm mittens. "Rain needs boots," she said. "Snow needs mittens." Then she caught one more snowflake on her red boot.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Eliana was three today. The big room had balloons. Outside the window, soft snow fell on the slide. Nobody played on it now. Inside, everyone was warm.

Mama brought the cake. On top were three little candles. "Why three?" Eliana asked. Papa lit them with a match. The flames grew tall. Eliana counted one, two, three. "One candle for each year," said Gran, cutting a thick slice of cake.

Eliana took a big breath. She blew hard. All three flames went out. The smoke curled up in thin grey lines. "The candles went out because I blew on them," she said. Everyone clapped. Eliana ate her thick piece of cake. Baby Theo banged his spoon. Papa said, "Happy birthday, Eliana!" Outside, the snow kept falling, slow and quiet, on the empty slide.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Riley ran to the park. Her blue hair clip fell off somewhere. She wanted to find it.

First she used her eyes. She looked by the swings. She looked under the bench. No clip. "Maybe my ears can help," she said. She stood very still. She heard kids laughing. She heard a dog bark. No clip sound. A clip does not make noise.

Then she used her nose. She sniffed the big flower bed. It smelled sweet. She sniffed the dirt. It smelled dirty, like rain. Still no clip. "A nose can not smell a clip," she said.

Riley sat down in the sand. She put out her hands. She touched the sand, bit by bit. The sand was warm and bumpy. Her fingers went left. Her fingers went right. Then something hard and smooth touched her skin. It was the blue clip!

"Mom, I found it with my hands!" said Riley.

Mom smiled. "Your eyes looked and looked. But fingers can feel what eyes can not see."

Riley put the clip back in her hair. Then she licked her ice cream. Yum. "Mom, does my tongue help too?" she asked, and took one more lick.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Elliot ran to his toy box. He wanted to play house. He found his little duck toy, his teddy, and a small blanket.

"Baby duck is cold," said Elliot. He wrapped the duck in the blanket. But the duck kept slipping out. It slid onto the floor. Thump. Elliot picked it up. He wrapped it again. Thump. The blanket was too big and too smooth.

Then Elliot had a big idea. He gave the duck a name. "Your name is Ducky," he said. He rolled the blanket tight, the way Mom rolled his sleeping bag. Ducky stayed snug. "Ducky is warm now," said Elliot. He clapped his hands.

Next, Ducky was hungry. Elliot found a play apple. It was red and juicy. "Here, Ducky," he said. He held it to the duck's beak. He made a little munch, munch sound. "Ducky likes juicy apples," said Elliot. He patted Ducky's head, just like Dad patted his head.

Teddy wanted a turn too. "You be the doctor," Elliot told Teddy. Teddy checked Ducky with a spoon. It was a very good spoon. The phone rang in the kitchen. It was Mom calling them for a real snack. Elliot hugged Ducky tight and ran. "Come on, Ducky! Snack time!"

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Isaiah went to the store with Mama. He wanted the big red balloon by the door. But a girl was there too. Her name was Mia. She wanted the red balloon too.

Mia grabbed the string. Isaiah grabbed the string too. The balloon bounced between them. "One balloon, two hands," said the store man. "You can take turns. First Mia holds it. Then Isaiah holds it."

Isaiah let go first. Mia held the balloon. She counted to ten. Then she gave the string to Isaiah. Isaiah held the red balloon. It felt full and light in his hand. He counted to ten too. Then he gave it back.

"Taking turns works," said Isaiah. "One holds it. Then the other one holds it. Nobody cries."

The store man smiled. He reached under the counter. He pulled out one more red balloon! "A full basket of balloons was hiding here," he said. Now Mia had one, and Isaiah had one. "We both keep a balloon," said Isaiah. He waved to Mia all the way to the street.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Grayson packed his little blue bag. In went one bear, two socks, three crackers. "Trip time!" he yelled. The car was full. Dad put the map in the front. Mom put the food in the back.

At the campsite, Grayson jumped out. He saw a spotted deer by the trees. He saw a big fire pit. He saw his own little tent. "I sleep here!" he said. But then Grayson felt sad. His bear was not in his bag. The bear was home, far away.

"We can make a new bear," said Mom. She took out paper and a pencil. They drew a bear with round ears. Grayson held the paper bear tight at bedtime. The tent went flap, flap in the wind. Grayson said, "The wind makes the tent move." He yawned and closed his eyes.

In the morning, Dad held up something soft. "Look who came with us!" It was the real bear, tucked in Dad's coat pocket all along. Grayson hugged the bear, then the paper bear too. "Two bears! One, two!"

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Charlotte rode her bike to the barbershop. Her dad walked beside her. This was her very first haircut.

The barber put a big cape on Charlotte. The cape was too big. It kept slipping off. "The clip is too weak," the barber said. "It cannot hold the cape." He got a strong clip instead. Now the cape stayed on.

The barber picked up his scissors. Then he stopped. Charlotte's hair was full of tangles. The tangles came from her bike helmet. "Why is my hair so tangled?" Charlotte asked. The helmet had rubbed on her hair on the ride.

The barber filled a spray bottle with water. He sprayed Charlotte's hair. Splash, splash. "Why does it need water?" she asked. He let her touch her wet hair. It felt soft now. The comb went right through it. Charlotte smiled. Wet hair was easy to comb.

The scissors went snip, snip, snip. Soon Charlotte had short, neat hair. "No more tangles," she said. "My hair is wet, so the comb can roll right through it."

Then she pedaled her bike all the way home.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Luke woke up early. Today was a big day. Grandma was coming for Eid.

Luke wanted to help make the sweet biscuits. But he could not reach the table. He got his little stool. Now he could reach!

Grandma showed him the dough. Luke could fold it over. He folded one piece. Then another. His hands were sticky. The dough was gone from the bowl. The bowl was empty.

"Grandma, no more dough!" said Luke.

Grandma smiled. "We made them all, Luke."

Soon the biscuits came out of the oven. They smelled so good. Luke counted them. One, two, three, all the way to ten.

The family sat together. Everyone ate the biscuits. Luke gave Grandma the biggest one.

Then Luke picked up crumbs. He put them in a small pile, like a little nest. "The crumbs fell because I ate fast," he said.

Grandma laughed. "Eat slower next time, little one."

Luke ate one more biscuit, slow slow slow. No crumbs fell. "Look, Grandma! I ate slow, so no crumbs!"

Grandma clapped her hands. "Yes, Luke. That is our clever boy."

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Hailey went to the grocery store with Dad. They walked past the apples. They walked past the bread. Then they came to the big cold door. Frost was on the glass.

"It is freezing in there," said Dad. "Put on your coat, Hailey."

Hailey pushed her arms in. One arm went in fast. The other arm hid. She shook the coat. She wiggled. Pop! The arm came out. "I did it!" she said.

Now the zipper. Hailey pulled it up. It would not zip. She pulled again. Nothing. "Why will it not zip?" she asked. She looked down. The zipper pull was way up high, not at the bottom. She slid it down, down, down. Then she pushed the two sides into the little slot together. She pulled up. Zip! It worked!

"Is that true? Did you zip it all alone?" asked Dad.

"Yes! The pull has to start at the bottom," said Hailey.

Dad hugged her. A silly snowman sticker fell out of her sleeve. "Where did he come from?" Hailey laughed. "He came to shop too!"

They bought milk for a drink and seeds for the garden. Hailey wore her coat all the way home.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Jayden sat at the paint table at summer camp. He wanted to paint a big orange ball, like the one he saw roll down the hill. But there was no orange paint. "No orange," said Jayden. His hands felt stuck.

Miss Rosa sat next to him. "Let's look at your paints," she said. "Red, yellow, blue. One, two, three." Jayden pointed. "Red, yellow, blue!" he said. The paint felt cool and wet on his fingers.

"Try red and yellow," said Miss Rosa. Jayden dipped his brush in red. Then he dipped it in yellow. He mixed them round and round. The bowl made a sloshy sound. "Look!" said Jayden. "Red and yellow make orange! They made orange because I mixed them!" He painted his ball. It was big and bright. "My ball!" he said. Miss Rosa smiled. "You made your own orange, Jayden."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Henri sat on the big train with Mama. He held his teddy bear tight. "Are we home yet?" he asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "The train takes us far away. We sleep at Grandma's house tonight."

Henri had a little carton of milk. He put it on the tray. Then the train began to move. Chug, chug! The milk carton wobbled. It tipped over! Milk ran all over the tray. Henri looked at it. "The milk fell because the train moved," he said. Mama smiled. "Yes, the train made it jump."

Mama wiped the milk with a napkin. She gave Henri a new carton. "Hold it in your hands this time," she said. Henri held it tight. The train went faster. The milk did not fall. "My hands are strong," said Henri. "The straw was weak before. It bent and fell too."

The train went chug, chug, chug. Trees went by the window. Henri saw a cow in a field. He waved at the cow. "Bye, cow!" he said. Mama waved too. Henri put his head on Mama's arm. The train went soft and rumbly. He watched the wheels go round and round. "Mama, is Grandma far?" he asked. "A little far," said Mama. "But the train knows the way." Henri hugged his teddy. His eyes closed slowly. The train went chug, chug, all the way.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Hudson sat at the little table in the art room. He wanted to paint a purple grape. He looked for purple paint. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was blue paint. There was no purple paint at all.

Miss Ana put a brush in his hand. "You can mix two paints," she said. Hudson dipped his brush in red. He dipped it in blue too. He made a dot on the paper. The dot was purple! "Red and blue make purple," he said.

Hudson tried again. He made another dot. It was purple too. He hummed a little song while he painted. Then he painted a big purple grape.

He wanted to make a green leaf next. He dipped his brush in yellow. He dipped it in blue. He made a dot. It was green! The paper got wet, so he had to wait. He waited and watched the paint dry.

Then he added one more dot with his fingernail scratch on the paper. "Look, my grape!" he said.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Alice sat in her car seat. The car went hum, hum, hum. "Are we at Grandma's now?" Alice said. "Not now," said Dad. "We get there later. Later comes after now." Alice watched the trees go by. One tree, then another tree, then another.

Alice had a bag on her lap. It was heavy. It had bread inside for Grandma. "Yesterday we made this bread," Alice said. "Yes," said Dad. "Yesterday is the day that is done. Today we drive. Tomorrow we play with Grandma." Alice put a berry in her mouth. It was sweet.

The sky got dark. Alice's eyes got heavy too. "Sleep now," said Dad. "Grandma later." Alice slept in her seat, soft and warm. The car went hum, hum, hum all night.

Alice woke up. The car was still. There was a door, and there was Grandma! "You slept a long time," said Grandma. "Now it is tomorrow!" Alice hugged her heavy bag. "The bread made yesterday is for today," Alice said. Grandma took the bread and smiled. "Come in," she said. "We will eat it now."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Everly could not sleep. She wanted tomorrow to come now. Tomorrow was Grandma's birthday party.

She got out of bed. She went to find Daddy. "Is it tomorrow yet?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Daddy. "First we sleep. Then it is tomorrow."

Everly drank some water from her cup. There was lemon in the water. She took a little taste. It was sour! She made a funny face. Daddy laughed softly.

"But I want tomorrow now," said Everly.

"Sleep comes first," said Daddy. "Yesterday we made the cake. Today we set the table. Tomorrow we will eat it."

Everly looked out the window. The moon was up now. The sun would come later. She got it. The moon goes, then the sun comes, then it is tomorrow.

She climbed back into bed. She hugged her bear. She closed her eyes. She waited and waited.

The room got light. The sun was up! Everly jumped out of bed. "The sun came!" she said. "Sleep went away. Now it is tomorrow!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Ellie sat at the dinner table. She tapped her spoon on her plate. Her peas rolled round and round.

"I want Grandma," said Ellie. "Is she coming now?"

"Not now," said Mom. "Grandma comes tomorrow."

Ellie frowned. Her tummy felt upset. Tomorrow was too far away.

"What is tomorrow?" asked Ellie.

Mom did not say. She started to fill her own plate. "Eat your peas first," she said.

Ellie looked at her spoon. She piled three peas on it. The spoon looked like a little green boat. She sailed the boat to her mouth. One, two, three. The peas were gone.

"Pea boat, pea boat," said Ellie. She made another boat. Then another.

The sky outside got dark. The lamp made a warm yellow circle on the table.

"Now it is night," said Mom. "Sleep comes at night. After sleep, it is tomorrow."

Ellie ate her last pea. She thought hard.

"So I sleep," she said, "and then it is tomorrow? Then Grandma comes?"

Mom smiled and nodded. Ellie slid down from her chair. She ran to find her pajamas.

"Come on, bed," she called. "Hurry up and be done."

She lay down and closed her eyes tight. In the morning, Grandma knocked at the door.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Dylan ran to the park with his red ball. The weather was warm and sunny. The grass smelled fresh and green.

He saw a girl on the swing. She was pushing her feet hard. Her mouth turned up. She was laughing loud. "She is happy," Dylan said. Then a boy dropped his ice cream. His mouth turned down. His eyes got wet. He was sad.

Dylan bounced his red ball. It went high. It went over the bushes. He could not see it. His tummy felt tight. He wanted to cry.

A big dog ran by. The dog barked. The sad boy jumped back. His eyes got wide. He was scared. The dog sniffed the bushes. Out came the red ball! The dog pushed it with his nose.

Dylan clapped his hands. His heart went fast, like a drum. He felt excited. He picked up his ball. "Good dog," he said. "You found it because you sniffed the bushes." The dog wagged his tail.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Anthony went to the library with Mama. He was hungry, so he held her hand tight.

"Story time is today," said Mama. "Yesterday we missed it. Today we are here!" Anthony put the book from yesterday on the desk. He heard the librarian say, "This book was due yesterday. Thank you for bringing it back." Anthony smiled. Yesterday was the day before today. Now he knew.

"Can we get a cake book now?" Anthony asked. "We can look now," said Mama. "We will read it later, at home." They found one, two, three cake books. Cake today, cake tomorrow, cake every day!

At home, Anthony turned the pages. "Look, Mama. We mix the cake now. We eat it later." He tapped the picture. "Later comes after now!"

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
knowledge_domain: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Sofia sat in the car with her teddy bear. "The dentist will count my teeth," she said to Mama. "One, two, three, teeth," she counted, tapping her teddy's smile. Mama smiled too.

At the dentist's office, Sofia sat on a wooden bench. It felt smooth and cool. A tall chair waited for her. Sofia could not reach the big chair by herself. The dentist helped her up. "Open wide," he said. Sofia opened her mouth. He counted out loud. "One, two, three," all the way to twenty. Sofia's teddy sat on her tummy. The dentist peeked in the teddy's ear too, and they both laughed.

"There, all clean," the dentist said. He gave Sofia a small sticker. In the car, Mama buckled her in. Sofia held up the sticker. "My teeth got counted," she said. "Twenty of them, Mama. Twenty."

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Michael was four years old. He went to school with his red backpack. Today his class would play outside. But first, everyone had to put on their shoes.

Michael felt shy. He sat alone by the wall. He pushed his feet into his shoes all by himself. The teacher smiled at him. Then Michael stood up to walk. Ouch! His feet felt funny. His toes bumped into each other. He fell down on the soft mat.

His friend Lily came over. "Try swapping your shoes," she said. Michael pulled the shoes off. He put the left shoe on his left foot. He put the right shoe on his right foot. He stood up again. He walked to the door. No ouch! No falling!

"The shoes hurt because they were on the wrong feet," Michael said. Lily clapped for him. Outside, they ran to the sandbox. Michael smelled the fresh bread from the kitchen. Lunch was coming soon. After lunch came a nap on his little mat.

Later, Michael drew a picture on the classroom computer. He drew two shoes. One said L and one said R. He showed it to his teacher. "I can put on my shoes all by myself now," he said. Then he wiggled his happy toes inside his right-way shoes.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family

story:
Baby Mia was crying. She was in her basket in the nursery.

Lincoln did not want her to cry. He did not want to be alone with the crying. He ran to find Mom. "Come quick," he said. Mom was feeding Mia soon.

"Maybe she is hungry," said Mom. "Babies cry when they need milk."

Linlin watched. Mom gave Mia milk. The crying stopped. Mia made small sounds. Her eyes closed.

Lincoln saw the answer. "She cried because she was hungry," he said. "Now she is full."

Mom smiled. "Yes. Now she can sleep."

Later Mia cried again. Lincoln was big now. He ran to fetch Mom. He did not say a word. He just pulled her hand. Mom picked up Mia.

"You told me," said Mom. "Good helper."

Lincoln patted Mia's soft blanket. It smelled like milk and soap. Mia yawned and went to sleep.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Aiden sat on the small red rug. His teacher had a big basket of books. Aiden picked one. He opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one. He went from the front to the back. On the last page was a picture of a brown dog. The teacher pointed at the words. "Those marks say good night, dog," she said. Aiden looked at the marks. The marks could talk!

The teacher said the books came from the library. "You can take one home," she said. Aiden wanted the dog book. He wanted to keep it forever. He hid it in his cubby. A boy named Sam looked in the basket. Sam wanted the dog book too. Sam got upset. "It's not here," he said. Aiden saw Sam's sad face.

Then Aiden had an idea. He lift ed the dog book out of his cubby. He gave it to the teacher. She put a paper card in it. "The card says bring it back," she said. Aiden took the book home. He read it front to back. On Friday, he brought it back. Sam smiled and hugged the book. "My turn," said Sam. Aiden clapped his hands.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Natalie ran into the nursery. A new baby was coming today! She wanted to give the baby a gift. She looked in her toy box. She found a red truck. She found a flat blue hat. Nothing felt just right.

Then Natalie saw her crayons. She could make a picture! She glued a photo of herself onto big paper. She added shiny stars. She made a road on the paper with a gray crayon. The road went right to the baby's crib. "This road shows the baby how to find me," she said.

The door opened. Mom carried in a tiny bundle. "Meet your baby brother," said Mom. Natalie tiptoed close. The baby's eyes opened. He looked at the paper. Then his mouth made a tiny O. Natalie giggled. "He likes the stars!"

Then something surprising happened. The baby grabbed Natalie's finger. He held on tight. Natalie laughed. "He is holding my hand because I am his sister," she said. She put the picture on the wall by his crib. The baby watched the stars shine. Natalie waved and said, "Goodnight, baby brother. I will see you tomorrow."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Austin sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted to hear his own heart. "Can I hear it?" he asked. The doctor smiled. She put small cups in Austin's ears. The cups had a long tube. "Now listen," she said. Austin heard a thump, thump, thump. "That is my heart!" he said. He heard it with his ears.

The doctor let him look at his skin with a tiny light. Austin saw his arm up close with his eyes. He touched a squishy ball on the table. His fingers felt it. He smelled a sticker that smelled like grapes. His nose knew it. The doctor gave him a candy. Austin tasted sweet on his tongue.

Austin gave his mother a grape sticker. "Your ears heard my heart," he said. "The cups made it loud." His mother laughed. Then Austin yawned a big yawn. "Sleepy," he said. The doctor said, "Big hearts need big naps." Austin closed his eyes right there in the chair.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Hunter was hungry for soup. Mom made a big pot of it. Hunter had a small bowl. Mom had a big bowl.

The sky outside was stormy. Rain tapped on the window. A little bird sat under the roof to stay dry.

Hunter blew on his soup. He blew fast. Then he blew slow. "Still hot!" he said. Mom sipped hers. "Mine is cold already," she said. Hunter looked. Her bowl was big and deep. His bowl was small and flat.

He waited a little more. The small bowl let the heat go out fast. Then he took a sip. "Cold enough!" he said. "My little bowl wins!"

Mom laughed. "My big bowl loses," she said. "But I get more soup."

Hunter slurped his soup. The rain went tap, tap, tap.
